clinicalPearls: Fertile eunuch syndrome (Pasqualini syndrome) is a variant of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism characterised by selective deficiency of luteinising hormone action with relatively preserved follicle-stimulating hormone, so some spermatogenesis occurs despite androgen deficiency.

The paradoxical name captures the picture of eunuchoid body proportions and delayed or incomplete virilisation, yet with sperm present in the tubules because intratubular support from FSH is comparatively intact.

The most specific molecular cause is a biallelic variant in LHB encoding the beta subunit of luteinising hormone, producing absent or bioinactive luteinising hormone; partial GnRH deficiency can produce a phenotypically similar picture.

Testes are often of relatively normal or only modestly reduced volume compared with classical hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, reflecting preserved FSH-driven tubular growth, but Leydig cell testosterone production is deficient.

The clinical clue is a eunuchoid habitus (arm span exceeding height, long lower segment) with low testosterone but detectable spermatogenesis and inappropriately low or bioinactive luteinising hormone.

Testosterone replacement corrects virilisation and eunuchoid symptoms; when fertility is desired, gonadotropin therapy (particularly luteinising hormone or chorionic gonadotropin activity) can restore Leydig cell function and improve conception prospects.

It sits within the broader spectrum of isolated gonadotropin deficiencies and must be distinguished from isolated FSH deficiency (FSHB) and from Kallmann syndrome, in which anosmia accompanies the hypogonadism.

Because the defect is one of hormone action rather than testicular failure, gonadotropins are low or inappropriately normal rather than elevated, distinguishing it from primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism.
reference.pathophysiology: Fertile eunuch syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in which luteinising hormone signalling is selectively deficient while follicle-stimulating hormone activity is relatively preserved. The most clearly defined molecular basis is a loss-of-function or bioinactivating variant in LHB, the gene encoding the beta subunit that confers biological specificity on luteinising hormone; the resulting hormone is either absent or unable to activate the luteinising hormone/chorionic gonadotropin receptor on testicular Leydig cells, so stimulated testosterone production fails. A phenotypically overlapping picture can arise from a partial deficiency of hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion that disproportionately affects luteinising hormone. Because follicle-stimulating hormone drives Sertoli cell function and the early stages of spermatogenesis, its relative preservation allows tubular development and some sperm production to continue, accounting for the retained testicular volume and residual fertility that give the syndrome its name. The androgen deficiency, however, impairs Leydig-cell-dependent virilisation and, by removing the pubertal signal for epiphyseal maturation, produces the characteristic eunuchoid skeletal proportions with a disproportionately long lower segment and arm span. Gonadotropin levels are low or inappropriately normal rather than elevated, confirming a central (hypogonadotropic) rather than primary gonadal mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Classical congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with combined LH and FSH deficiency
Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia; ANOS1, FGFR1 and others)
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism such as Klinefelter syndrome
Acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from pituitary tumour, hyperprolactinaemia or infiltrative disease
Androgen insensitivity and defects of testosterone biosynthesis
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone with luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone to demonstrate low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins
Semen analysis to document residual spermatogenesis
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation testing to assess pituitary gonadotrope responsiveness
Assessment of luteinising hormone bioactivity where available
Molecular genetic testing of LHB and related gonadotropin and GnRH pathway genes
Testicular volume measurement and scrotal ultrasound
Pituitary imaging and prolactin to exclude acquired central causes
redFlags: Failure to progress through puberty with eunuchoid proportions requiring endocrine evaluation
Low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins pointing to a central defect
Symptomatic androgen deficiency with reduced bone mineral density
Infertility in a man with detectable but suboptimal spermatogenesis
Features suggesting an acquired pituitary lesion (headache, visual field loss, other hormone deficiencies)
reference.prognosis: With testosterone replacement, virilisation, sexual function and bone health are restored, and gonadotropin therapy can achieve fertility in a substantial proportion because spermatogenesis is partially preserved. Long-term outlook is good provided androgen deficiency is treated and bone density protected.
pitfalls: Assuming a eunuchoid, undervirilised man is necessarily infertile and not offering semen analysis or gonadotropin therapy
Confusing the low-gonadotropin (central) picture with primary testicular failure, which shows raised gonadotropins
Using testosterone replacement alone when fertility is desired, as exogenous androgen suppresses residual gonadotropins and spermatogenesis
Overlooking anosmia, which would reclassify the disorder as Kallmann syndrome
Failing to protect bone health during periods of untreated androgen deficiency
references: Reference on disorders of male reproduction
Clinical genetics reference on gonadotropin deficiency
management: Give testosterone replacement to induce and maintain virilisation, sexual function, muscle mass and bone health when fertility is not currently sought

Use gonadotrophin therapy, supplying luteinising hormone activity with human chorionic gonadotrophin and adding follicle-stimulating hormone where needed, to stimulate Leydig-cell testosterone production and spermatogenesis when fertility is desired
Monitor testosterone response, virilisation, haematocrit and prostate health while on androgen replacement
Undertake bone mineral density surveillance and treat osteoporosis risk arising from androgen deficiency
Document and track spermatogenesis with semen analysis during gonadotrophin therapy, using assisted reproduction or sperm retrieval if required
Refer to reproductive endocrinology and fertility services for conception planning
Offer genetic counselling and testing given the LHB (autosomal recessive) molecular basis
